clue.text: One of two claimants to the throne of Barataria…

definitions.text: One of two claimants to the throne of Barataria…

parts.words: One of two claimants to the throne of Barataria…
parts.note: in Gilbert and Sullivan's comic opera, two Venetian boatmen, Marco and Giuseppe, jointly claim the throne of the imaginary kingdom of Barataria

explanation.surface: A trivia question about a disputed royal succession in a faraway kingdom.
explanation.walkthrough: The trailing dots run on into 6-across. Barataria is the kingdom in Gilbert and Sullivan's The Gondoliers, whose two heroes are Venetian boatmen.
explanation.definitionFit: Each of the two would-be kings in the Savoy opera is a Venetian boatman by trade.

clue.text: Wordsworth sends his sister for one awaited on stage

parts.note: to send someone away is to tell them to go
the poet Wordsworth's sister was Dorothy, Dot for short

explanation.surface: The poet packs his sister off in search of someone who is expected in the theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: Wordsworth's sister was Dorothy; the poet telling her 'go, Dot' gives the title character of Beckett's Waiting for Godot, who never arrives.
explanation.definitionFit: In Beckett's play two tramps wait endlessly for this character, who never turns up.

clue.text: Irritated by prophylactic treatment?

explanation.surface: Someone annoyed by their preventive medicine.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading is a pun: a vaccination is given with a hypodermic, so someone treated that way has been jabbed.
explanation.definitionFit: Irritated means riled or provoked; prophylactic treatment such as a vaccination is given by injection with a sharp hypodermic.

clue.text: Exhausted — like miserable Mr Micawber's annual income?

definitions.text: like miserable Mr Micawber's annual income?

explanation.surface: A tired person compared with Dickens's debt-ridden optimist.
explanation.walkthrough: Micawber in David Copperfield says an income of twenty pounds with spending of twenty pounds and sixpence results in misery: the income has been exceeded.
explanation.definitionFit: Exhausted funds are used up entirely; Micawber's yearly income was exceeded by his spending, making him miserable.

clue.text: Hamlet told Ophelia he was so honest

definitions.text: Hamlet told Ophelia he was so honest

parts.words: Hamlet told Ophelia he was so honest
parts.note: in the nunnery scene Hamlet tells Ophelia 'I am myself' only moderately honest, using an adjective that once meant fairly or passably

explanation.surface: A line about what the Danish prince said of his own integrity to Ophelia.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet's words are 'I am myself indifferent honest', where the adjective means 'moderately'; the solver needs the modern sense of not caring.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's usage the word meant middling or passable, while today it means unconcerned.

clue.text: Hood dropped in to do so

indicators.note: the word in is dropped from the outlaw's first name, so those two letters go

parts.note: Robin Hood, the outlaw of Sherwood Forest
taken as written

explanation.surface: The famous outlaw dropped in on someone in order to steal from them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hood' is Robin Hood, the English folk outlaw who stole from the rich; 'dropped in' looks like visiting but removes IN from ROBIN. 'To do so' means to do what Robin Hood did.
explanation.definitionFit: Robin Hood's trade was theft from the rich, so doing as he did means stealing.

clue.text: … changing roles with the unsuccessful one?

indicators.note: changing the order of the letters of the word roles makes a new word

explanation.surface: The two claimants swapping parts, one taking the role of the failure.
explanation.walkthrough: The dots continue the story from 1-across. 'changing' rearranges ROLES.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who fails to win a contest is defeated, the opposite of a winner.

clue.text: Wealth gave one of the Borgias a start

indicators.note: only a start of the name is wanted, so its closing letters are cut away

parts.note: Lucrezia Borgia, the Renaissance noblewoman

explanation.surface: Riches gave one of the notorious Italian family a head start in life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a start' keeps only the opening of LUCREZIA, dropping ZIA to leave the first five letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is an old, often disapproving term for money or riches, as in 'filthy' money.

clue.text: Where Greeks gave Persians beans — or sausages?

explanation.surface: A history question about a Greek victory, with a culinary afterthought.
explanation.walkthrough: The Greek fleet defeated the Persians at the sea battle of Salamis in 480 BC; to give someone beans is to beat them soundly. The same letters are the plural of an Italian sausage.
explanation.definitionFit: The island off Athens was the site of the famous naval victory over Xerxes; spiced Italian sausages share the name.

clue.text: Teller of tales — a French one in Capek's play

indicators.note: the word in tells us the French tale is placed inside the play's title

parts.note: R.U.R. is Karel Capek's play which introduced the word robot
taken as written
one refers back to tales, and conte is French for a tale

explanation.surface: A storyteller, perhaps a Frenchman, appearing in a Czech play.
explanation.walkthrough: R.U.R. (Rossum's Universal Robots) is Karel Capek's 1920 play. 'One' stands for a tale, so a French one is A CONTE, which goes in R.U.R.
explanation.definitionFit: A skilled storyteller, especially in conversation, is a raconteur.

clue.text: A sink-or-swim situation for inexperienced entrants

definitions.text: A sink-or-swim situation for inexperienced entrants

parts.words: A sink-or-swim situation for inexperienced entrants
parts.note: reads like a newcomer thrown into a demanding job, but literally describes the part of a swimming pool where a beginner may sink

explanation.surface: Newcomers to a job being left to sink or swim.
explanation.walkthrough: To be thrown in at this end of a pool is the idiom for taking on something difficult with no preparation.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for a challenging situation faced without experience comes from the part of a pool beyond one's depth.

clue.text: Rustic going blue at odd .intervals with stomach trouble

indicators.note: taking the first and third letters of blue, the odd-numbered positions

parts.note: colic is abdominal pain

explanation.surface: A countryman turning blue now and then with a bellyache.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at odd intervals' picks B and U from BLUE; 'going' and 'with' are joining words.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes country life, especially shepherds and pastoral scenes.

clue.text: Part of a skeleton in hospital use

indicators.note: the bone is found sitting within the letters of the words hospital use

explanation.surface: A bone being used in a hospital for teaching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' signals the run of letters across 'hospital use'.
explanation.definitionFit: The ankle bone, which joins the foot to the shin, is one of the bones of the skeleton.

clue.text: Saint Peter of the Papal Ring (if backed by the general)

definitions.text: Saint Peter of the Papal Ring

indicators.note: the word if is turned round, read backwards

parts.note: taken as written before reversal
William Tecumseh Sherman, the US Civil War general

explanation.surface: A remark about the Pope's ring, with a hedging aside about military support.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backed' reverses the little word; 'by' places the American Civil War general after it. The Pope's signet ring bears this title of Saint Peter, who was a Galilean net-caster.
explanation.definitionFit: Saint Peter worked the nets on Galilee before being called, and the Pope's signet ring is named after that trade.

clue.text: Tea's cheaper anyhow, and it's warmer indoors

indicators.note: anyhow means in any old way, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Tea is cheaper either way, and it warms you up inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anyhow' rearranges the letters of TEAS CHEAPER.
explanation.definitionFit: An electric or gas appliance that warms a room is a heater for the space.

clue.text: Anyway this bomb presents no danger

indicators.note: it reads the same whichever way you go, forwards or backwards

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: Whatever happens, this bomb is harmless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Anyway' says the word reads the same in either direction; a bomb that presents no danger is one that fails to go off.
explanation.definitionFit: A shell or bomb that fails to explode is a failure, a common term for any flop.

clue.text: Make unholy mess of seed packing-case

indicators.note: a mess of the letters of seed means they are jumbled

parts.note: a crate is a packing case

explanation.surface: Making an unholy mess of a box of seeds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mess of' jumbles the seed letters, which go before the box. 'Unholy mess' looks like a phrase but splits at the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To violate something sacred is to profane it.

clue.text: Its neighbour also' a "precious stone set in the silver sea"

definitions.text: Its neighbour also' a "precious stone set in the silver sea"

parts.words: Its neighbour also' a "precious stone set in the silver sea"
parts.note: John of Gaunt's speech in Richard II calls England a precious stone set in the silver sea; the island next door is likewise a green gem in the sea

explanation.surface: Quoting Shakespeare's praise of England and applying it to the country next door.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation is John of Gaunt on England in Richard II. Ireland, its neighbour, is also a 'precious stone', named after a green gem.
explanation.definitionFit: Ireland is nicknamed after a green gemstone for its lush countryside.

clue.text: Devil's work getting fish without one on a great lake

indicators.note: without means outside here, so the fish's letters surround the numeral

parts.note: a dab is a flatfish
I is the Roman numeral for one
L abbreviates lake, followed by Erie, one of North America's Great Lakes

explanation.surface: Something devilish happening on an American lake when an angler catches a fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' is used in its old sense of 'outside', so the flatfish goes round the Roman one; 'on' is a joining word.
explanation.definitionFit: Diabolical mischief or sorcery is devilry.

clue.text: As in the lane perhaps where Napoleon last walked

indicators.note: perhaps suggests these words could be rearranged into something else

explanation.surface: A picture of Napoleon taking his final stroll down a country lane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges AS IN THE LANE. Napoleon died in exile on this South Atlantic island in 1821.
explanation.definitionFit: The remote South Atlantic island was Napoleon's final place of exile, where he died.

clue.text: Short measure — examination shows it's wrong

annotationWithheld.why: Short measure — examination shows it's wrong (7) for IMMORAL: ORAL is the examination, but no reading of 'Short measure' gives IMM (MM for millimetre leaves the I unaccounted for); clue matches the scan.
annotationWithheld.clue: Short measure — examination shows it's wrong

clue.text: Lawyers save a bit of music

explanation.surface: Lawyers protecting a snippet of music.
explanation.walkthrough: Three meanings: barristers collectively, 'except' as a preposition, and a measure of music.
explanation.definitionFit: Barristers as a body form this profession; save in the sense of except; and a measure in a musical score.

clue.text: A way to support terrorist weapon with high-flown talk

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting pieces sit below the weapon

parts.note: a bomb is a terrorist's weapon
ST is short for street, a way

explanation.surface: A method of backing a terrorist's armament with grandiose rhetoric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to support' means A and ST go below BOMB in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Pompous, inflated language with little substance is bombast.

clue.text: Some club members take care of double-time adjustment without one

parts.note: c/o is the postal abbreviation for care of

indicators.note: an adjustment rearranges the letters that remain
without one means a single numeral I is taken away
double means the word time is written twice

parts.note: taken as written
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A club official agrees to take care of fixing overtime pay without a single member.
explanation.walkthrough: 'double' writes the word twice; 'without one' removes an I; 'adjustment' jumbles the remaining TMETIME, placed after the postal abbreviation. 'take' is a joining word.
explanation.definitionFit: A small group chosen from a society's membership to run its business is a committee.

clue.text: East River's sort of revolution without trial

indicators.note: without means the word trial is removed

parts.note: the Industrial Revolution
taken as written

explanation.surface: An Eastern waterway's take on a revolution that came without a trial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'East River' looks like the New York waterway, but means a river in the East. 'without' takes TRIAL from INDUSTRIAL.
explanation.definitionFit: The great river of Pakistan flows through South Asia, the East.

clue.text: Arboreal type of bird caught by both sides

indicators.note: caught by means the bird is held inside the letters for the two sides

parts.note: L and R stand for left and right
the emu is a large flightless Australian bird

explanation.surface: A tree-dwelling bird trapped from both sides.
explanation.walkthrough: 'caught by' puts EMU between L and R (left and right).
explanation.definitionFit: The Madagascan primate lives in the trees, a tree-dwelling animal.

clue.text: Almost literally the last apartment suitable for swinging cats

parts.note: a room is an apartment in the old sense of a chamber
the last letter of the alphabet is Z, and the one almost at the end is Y

explanation.surface: Searching for a final flat big enough to swing a cat in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'literally' means 'in letters': the last letter is Z, so almost the last is Y. 'Room to swing a cat' is the idiom for space.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'room to swing a cat' describes a spacious place, so this means spacious.

clue.text: Make short work of a game

parts.note: bridge is a card game

explanation.surface: Polishing off a game quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition means shorten a work such as a book; 'of' is a joining word.
explanation.definitionFit: To condense a book or text is to shorten it.

clue.text: One of the flock would you say?

indicators.note: would ... say frames the pronoun as a question about how something is spoken
say asks how the word is spoken, signalling a sound-alike

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A question asking whether someone counts as one of the congregation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'would ... say' wraps the pronoun and signals a sound-alike for it.
explanation.definitionFit: A female sheep is a member of a flock.

clue.text: Rent trouble — a big blow

parts.note: rent as a past participle means torn
ado is fuss or trouble

explanation.surface: A dispute over rent, then a heavy blow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rent' looks like a payment to a landlord but is the past of rend, to tear.
explanation.definitionFit: A violent rotating windstorm is a huge gust of wind.

clue.text: American island where lisle is : 'woven

indicators.note: woven suggests the letters of lisle are interlaced into a new order

explanation.surface: A place in America where lisle cotton thread is woven.
explanation.walkthrough: 'woven' rearranges LISLE. The island is the immigration station in New York Harbor.
explanation.definitionFit: The island in New York Harbor was the main US immigrant inspection station.

clue.text: In serious vein, like bird catching worms round his retreat

indicators.note: round means the bird's adjective goes around the retreat

parts.note: the proverb says the early bird catches the worm
the bird's retreat is its nest

explanation.surface: A bird earnestly catching worms around its home.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'the early bird catches the worm' supplies the adjective, which goes 'round' the bird's home.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting with sincere, solemn intent is the manner described.
